Resource Minimum OS Linux with KVM and nested virt (if host is a VM) RAM ~18 GiB (rancher-test) or ~30 GiB (rancher) available Disk ~130 GiB (rancher-test) or ~220 GiB (rancher) free in /var/lib/libvirt/images CPU ~8 (rancher-test) or ~14 (rancher) vCPU to spare Python 3.10+

Run rodeo doctor to check your host and confirm this profile fits.

docs.title: Deploy
docs.text:
rodeo up --profile rancher        # or: rodeo up --profile rancher-test

rodeo up checks the host, installs any missing packages (with your consent), generates credentials, and starts the deploy. It self-escalates with sudo: you do not need to prefix sudo yourself.

rodeo up wraps itself in a tmux session (rodeo-rancher) automatically, so a dropped SSH connection does not kill the deploy. Re-attach with tmux attach -t rodeo-rancher. Use --no-tmux to skip this in scripts.

If rodeo up is already installed and you have already run install-deps once:

rodeo up --profile rancher --yes    # skip all prompts

docs.title: What happens during deploy
docs.text:
The pipeline runs these phases in order:

  1. kvm_host: sets up libvirt, firewall rules, and the storage pool on the host
  2. vms: downloads the cloud image, injects cloud-init, creates the VM disks and libvirt definitions
  3. boot: starts the libvirt network and the VMs (no PXE wait needed)
  4. rancher: waits for the Rancher VM to get an IP, installs K3s, deploys Rancher Prime via Helm, waits for the UI to become healthy
  5. downstream: creates each downstream cluster in Rancher, registers its nodes, and waits until every cluster is Ready
  6. finalise: enables VM autostart on host reboot (skipped on Instruqt; use rodeo start-if-needed on hostimage boot instead of baking finalise into the image)

Total time: about 20-40 minutes on a typical host. Most of it is Rancher provisioning the downstream clusters; the 3-node RKE2 cluster joins one node at a time.

docs.title: Log in
docs.text:
After rodeo up finishes it prints the Rancher URL and credentials. If you need them again:

rodeo status
  • URL: https://<host-ip>:30002
  • Username: admin
  • Password: the value of rancher_admin_password in ~/.rodeo/secrets.yaml

First login will prompt you to confirm the server URL. Use the host IP (the one shown in rodeo status), not localhost.

docs.title: Day-2 operations
docs.text: Task Command Check VM and service health rodeo status SSH into the Rancher VM rodeo ssh rancher SSH into a downstream node rodeo ssh k3s, rodeo ssh rke2-ha1, ... Tail serial log rodeo logs rancher Restart the VM rodeo restart rancher Graceful stop rodeo stop --all --yes Start after stop rodeo start --all --yes Destroy the lab rodeo clean --yes Full host reset rodeo clean --all --yes --secrets

docs.title: Resume a failed deploy
docs.text:
rodeo status                    # find the last failed phase
rodeo deploy --from rancher     # resume from that phase

docs.title: Instruqt workflow
docs.text: Set deployment_target: instruqt in rodeo-plan.yaml before deploying so finalise is skipped. Do not bake finalise into a hostimage (autostart can hang the Instruqt agent / console). After deploy, follow the success-screen checklist, Save the hostimage, and put rodeo start-if-needed in the track setup script so the lab comes up on every boot. See Instruqt example.

docs.title: Customize
docs.text:
All settings live in ~/.rodeo/profiles/rancher/ (if deployed via --profile) or your local lab dir.

Override resources at deploy time:

rodeo deploy -P resources.rancher.memory_mib=12288
rodeo deploy -P resources.rancher.vcpu=6
rodeo deploy -P resources.rke2-node.memory_mib=6144   # every RKE2 node

The clusters, and which VM joins which, are in definition.yaml (downstream_clusters and nodes).

To make a modified copy you can edit and redeploy:

rodeo new myrancher --from rancher
$EDITOR ~/.rodeo/profiles/myrancher/rodeo-plan.yaml
rodeo up --profile myrancher

Full format reference: Create your own rodeo.

docs.title: SUSE Edge 3.7: profile guide
docs.text:
This guide covers the suse-edge profile: a full SUSE Edge 3.7 stack on nested KVM. It stands up a Rancher Prime management cluster with the Elemental Operator, an Edge Image Builder (EIB) VM, and a set of Elemental-managed edge nodes, the pieces you need to demo zero-touch edge onboarding end to end.

Use it when the workshop or demo focuses on edge lifecycle: building an OS image with EIB, then registering edge nodes into Rancher over TPM with Elemental.

docs.title: What you get
docs.text:
Component Default IP Access Rancher Prime (management cluster) 192.168.122.9 https://rancher.<host-ip>.sslip.io (Traefik + Let's Encrypt) Edge Image Builder (EIB) 192.168.122.20 rodeo ssh eib edge1 192.168.122.31 rodeo ssh edge1 edge2 192.168.122.32 rodeo ssh edge2 edge3 192.168.122.33 rodeo ssh edge3 edge4 192.168.122.34 rodeo ssh edge4

Rancher is reached through Traefik ingress, not a NodePort: cert-manager gets a real Let's Encrypt certificate over the HTTP01 challenge (port 80), and the UI + API + Elemental registration endpoint are served on port 443 at a sslip.io hostname derived from the host's external IP. Edge nodes are created by the vms phase but started as a lab exercise, not automatically, that is the hands-on part of the workshop.

Component versions (SUSE Edge 3.7): Rancher Prime 2.15.1 on K3s v1.36.3+k3s1 (lab) · cert-manager v1.20.1 · Elemental Operator 1.9.2 · Elemental UI extension 3.0.3 · Edge Image Builder 1.3.4.

docs.title: Host requirements
docs.text:
Resource Minimum OS Linux with KVM and nested virt (if host is a VM) RAM ~40 GiB available Disk ~200 GiB free in /var/lib/libvirt/images CPU ~8 vCPU to spare Extras swtpm for the virtual TPM 2.0 on edge nodes (installed by install-deps) Python 3.10+

The host also needs inbound ports 80 and 443 reachable from where you browse, so Let's Encrypt can complete the ACME challenge and you can reach the Rancher UI.

Run rodeo doctor to check your host and confirm this profile fits.

docs.title: On AWS
docs.text:
rodeo up --profile suse-edge --target aws --yes

rodeo's AWS security group only opens 22, 8443 and 30002 to your IP, so Let's Encrypt cannot run there. On AWS rodeo switches Rancher to its own certificate on https://<host>:30002 (accept the browser warning) and gives the Rancher and EIB VMs more RAM and disk. The recommended instance is m8id.4xlarge, and the host has the usual 6-hour dead-man switch.

docs.title: Deploy
docs.text:
rodeo up --profile suse-edge

rodeo up checks the host, installs any missing packages (with your consent), generates credentials, and starts the deploy. It self-escalates with sudo: you do not need to prefix sudo yourself.

rodeo up wraps itself in a tmux session (rodeo-suse-edge) automatically, so a dropped SSH connection does not kill the deploy. Re-attach with tmux attach -t rodeo-suse-edge. Use --no-tmux to skip this in scripts.

docs.title: What happens during deploy
docs.text:
The pipeline runs these phases in order:

  1. kvm_host: sets up libvirt, firewall rules (including the 80/443 DNAT), swtpm, and the storage pool on the host
  2. vms: downloads the base images, injects cloud-init, creates the Rancher, EIB, and edge node disks and libvirt definitions
  3. boot: starts the libvirt network and the Rancher + EIB VMs (edge nodes stay off for the lab exercise)
  4. rancher: installs K3s, deploys Rancher Prime via Helm, and configures cert-manager + Traefik for the Let's Encrypt certificate
  5. elemental: installs the Elemental Operator (CRDs + Operator) and creates the MachineRegistration so edge nodes can register over TPM
  6. apply: applies any extra manifests (Fleet GitOps, demo workloads)
  7. finalise: enables VM autostart on host reboot (skipped on Instruqt; use rodeo start-if-needed on hostimage boot instead of baking finalise into the image)

Total time: 20–40 minutes on a typical host, depending on image download speed.

docs.title: Log in
docs.text:
After rodeo up finishes it prints the Rancher URL and credentials. If you need them again:

rodeo status
  • URL: https://rancher.<host-ip>.sslip.io
  • Username: admin
  • Password: the value of rancher_admin_password in ~/.rodeo/secrets.yaml

Because Rancher is served with a real Let's Encrypt certificate, there is no browser warning to click through, but the host must be reachable on ports 80 and 443 from the public internet for the certificate to issue.

docs.title: The edge lab exercise
docs.text:
The edge nodes are the point of this profile. After the deploy finishes:

  1. On the EIB VM, build an Elemental OS image (SelfInstall ISO for edge1/edge2, Default RAW for edge3/edge4).
  2. Start an edge node and boot it from that image: rodeo restart edge1, then watch it with rodeo logs edge1.
  3. The node registers into Rancher over its virtual TPM via the Elemental MachineRegistration.
  4. Watch it appear under Cluster Management → Machine Inventory in the Rancher UI.

Tune how many registrations exist with elemental.registrations in the plan.

docs.title: Day-2 operations
docs.text: Task Command Check VM and service health rodeo status SSH into a VM rodeo ssh rancher / rodeo ssh eib / rodeo ssh edge1 Tail serial log rodeo logs edge1 Start an edge node rodeo restart edge1 Graceful stop rodeo stop --all --yes Start after stop rodeo start --all --yes Destroy the lab rodeo clean --yes Full host reset rodeo clean --all --yes --secrets

docs.title: Resume a failed deploy
docs.text:
rodeo status                      # find the last failed phase
rodeo deploy --from elemental     # resume from that phase

docs.title: Instruqt workflow
docs.text: Set deployment_target: instruqt in rodeo-plan.yaml before deploying so finalise is skipped. Do not bake finalise into a hostimage (autostart can hang the Instruqt agent / console). After deploy, follow the success-screen checklist, Save the hostimage, and put rodeo start-if-needed in the track setup script so the lab comes up on every boot. See Instruqt example.

docs.title: Customize
docs.text:
All settings live in ~/.rodeo/profiles/suse-edge/ (if deployed via --profile) or your local lab dir.

Override resources or edge behaviour at deploy time:

rodeo deploy -P resources.rancher.memory_mib=12288
rodeo deploy -P rancher_tls.email=me@example.com
rodeo deploy -P elemental.registrations=2

To make a modified copy you can edit and redeploy:

rodeo new myedge --from suse-edge
$EDITOR ~/.rodeo/profiles/myedge/rodeo-plan.yaml
rodeo up --profile myedge

Full format reference: Create your own rodeo.

docs.title: SUSE Telco Cloud 3.7: profile guide
docs.text:
--profile suse-telco builds the infrastructure for the SUSE Telco Cloud 3.7 workshop (Northline). rodeo stands up the management cluster, an emulated Redfish BMC, the downstream image, and enrolls the site hosts. It stops there. Students apply the workshop's manifests/ themselves.

The bundled plan and the copy in avaleror/suse-telco-workshop must stay identical. rodeo up --target aws seeds the EC2 host from the copy in this repo.

docs.title: What you get
docs.text:
VM Default IP Role mgmt 192.168.122.10 RKE2 management cluster, Rancher site-co 192.168.122.21 Site host. Metal3 powers it site-ran 192.168.122.32 Site host site-co-2 192.168.122.23 Site host site-co-3 192.168.122.24 Site host

DNS domain: northline.telco. Gateway: 192.168.122.1.

Guest sizes in the bundled plan: mgmt 8 vCPU / 16 GiB / 80 GiB disk, each site host 4 vCPU / 8 GiB / 40 GiB disk.

Component versions (SUSE Telco Cloud 3.7.0 release notes): Rancher 2.15.1 · RKE2 v1.36.3+rke2r1 · cert-manager v1.20.1 · Turtles providers chart 307.0.8+up0.27.0 · Metal3 chart 307.0.31+up0.16.0 · MetalLB 307.0.3+up0.16.1 · Longhorn 1.12.1 · Edge Image Builder 1.3.4. Helm components are chart versions. KubeVirt (chart 307.0.3+up0.8.0) is for lab 07.

docs.title: Editions
docs.text:
edition in the plan picks the base image and the Rancher chart repo. The Telco Cloud pins stay the same.

edition Built from Who fetches the base image product (default) SUSE Linux Micro 6.2 + Rancher Prime You. Stage SL-Micro.x86_64-6.2-Base-GM.raw.xz, or set telco.base_image.url opensource openSUSE Leap Micro 6.2 + community Rancher rodeo downloads it

Neither edition needs an SCC registration code. If credentials.scc_registration_code is set on the product edition, the downstream image is built from SUSE repositories instead of the public SLE BCI repo.

On --target aws the instance's NVMe is mounted over /var/lib/libvirt/images, so a file you copied onto the host before rodeo up is hidden. Set telco.base_image.url (a presigned link in the same region works).

docs.title: Deploy
docs.text:
rodeo up --profile suse-telco
rodeo up --profile suse-telco --target aws --yes
rodeo up --profile suse-telco --target gcp --yes

Bare metal is the plan default. --target wins and is written back into the plan.

The catalog's recommended cloud size is a starting point, not a measured pin: AWS m8id.4xlarge (16 vCPU / 64 GiB / local NVMe) for labs 01–06. The performance tier is the metal size, for nested KubeVirt in lab 07. GCP recommended is c4-standard-16-lssd.

docs.title: What rodeo runs
docs.text:
1. kvm_host: KVM, libvirt, firewall, storage
  2. vms: libvirt network, the mgmt disk from the SL Micro or Leap Micro image plus a combustion seed, blank site disks, domain XML
  3. bmc: sushy-tools, the emulated Redfish BMC for the site hosts
  4. boot: starts mgmt only. Metal3 owns power for the site hosts
  5. mgmt: installs the management stack
  6. images: builds the downstream image with EIB on the KVM host and publishes it to the mgmt image cache
  7. enroll: registers the site hosts as BareMetalHosts and waits until they are available
  8. finalise and custom_scripts

The lab is ready for students after enroll. finalise and custom_scripts still run after that. finalise is skipped when deployment_target is instruqt, same as the other profiles. Applying manifests/ is the student's job. In the workshop repo that starts with kubectl apply -f manifests/site-co.yaml (lab 04).

docs.title: Install on Linux and macOS
docs.text:
rodeo runs in two roles, and they have different platform rules:

Role What it does Linux macOS KVM host Runs the lab itself: rodeo up, status, stop, clean, ... Yes (SLES 16 / Leap 16 recommended) No Control machine Drives remote hosts: rodeo up --target aws, rodeo fleet ..., rodeo fleet portal ..., rodeo ssh Yes Yes

A Mac can never be a KVM host: labs need /dev/kvm, libvirt and Linux /proc. rodeo doctor on a Mac reports 0 GiB RAM and no /dev/kvm, which is expected. Everything else (cloud hosts, fleets, the claim portal) works the same from either platform.

docs.title: One installer, two roles
docs.text:
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/avaleror/rodeo-cli/main/install.sh | bash

install.sh looks at the machine and picks the role:

Machine Role What it installs SLES 16 / Leap 16 KVM host Needs root. python3, pip and git with zypper, rodeo in /opt/rodeo-cli, /usr/local/bin/rodeo. Then: rodeo up macOS, SLES/Leap 15, Ubuntu, Fedora, any other Linux Control machine No system packages and no root needed. rodeo with the [aws,gcp] extras in ~/.local/share/rodeo-cli, ~/.local/bin/rodeo (as root: /opt/rodeo-cli, /usr/local/bin). Then: rodeo up --profile <name> --target aws (or --target gcp)

On a control machine the installer uses a Python 3.10+ that is already there (Homebrew, python311 on SLES 15, ...). If there is none, for example the Python 3.9 of macOS or the 3.6 of SLES 15, it fetches a private Python with a pinned uv into the install directory. The system Python is never touched and no shell profile is edited; the installer prints the PATH line to add if ~/.local/bin is not on it yet.

It needs git and curl. On macOS they come with the Xcode command line tools (xcode-select --install); on Linux, as root, the installer adds them itself.

  • By default it installs the latest validated release: the version that last passed a live deploy, recorded in the STABLE file. A release tagged after it isn't installed until it passes too (how releases are validated).
  • --ref <tag|branch|sha> installs something else: a specific release (--ref v0.33.0), or --ref main for the latest code.
  • --mode kvm-host|control-plane (or RODEO_MODE) overrides the automatic choice, for example a KVM host on another distribution at your own risk.
  • --no-builder (or RODEO_BUILDER=0) skips the Rodeo Builder service and removes one an earlier install set up. --builder-host ADDR (or RODEO_BUILDER_HOST) sets the address it listens on (default 0.0.0.0).
  • Re-running the installer updates rodeo. An environment left on a Python that is too old is rebuilt.

You normally never run it by hand on cloud hosts: rodeo up --target aws and rodeo fleet deploy run it on the host for you.

On a control machine, rodeo up without --target aws, --target gcp, or --target remote stops and says so instead of starting a lab it cannot run (--no-deploy still sets the lab up). RODEO_ALLOW_ANY_KVM_HOST=1 lets you try a local lab on an unsupported Linux anyway.

docs.title: Rodeo Builder service
docs.text:
On Linux with systemd, in both roles, the installer runs the Rodeo Builder as rodeo-builder.service, so https://<this host>:8678/ is up after the install and after every reboot. It runs rodeo builder --no-open --host 0.0.0.0 --expose, listening on every interface over HTTPS (a certificate signed by rodeo's own CA; import https://<this host>:8678/ca.pem once in each browser, see Rodeo Builder), and is restarted on every update, by the installer and by rodeo self-update (--no-restart skips it), so it always runs the code just installed. A server left running on older code keeps serving the page it read at start-up while handing out the new scripts, and the page then fails to open.

On every interface the builder answers to this machine's host names and the addresses on its interfaces, read each time it starts; any other Host is refused, so other sites still can't reach it through DNS rebinding. Add names clients use that the machine can't see itself (a DNS alias, a public IP behind NAT) with RODEO_BUILDER_ALLOW="name1 name2".

Exposed, anyone who can reach port 8678 can save profiles as the service's user; Deploy and stored credentials ask for a login (rodeo logins add <user>, see Settings page), and Publish uses the github.com pages instead of this host's GitHub login (see Rodeo Builder). Limit who reaches the port with your firewall, or keep it on this machine with --builder-host 127.0.0.1 and tunnel (ssh -L 8678:127.0.0.1:8678 <host>).

Installed as Unit file Manage with root /etc/systemd/system/rodeo-builder.service (runs as root) systemctl status rodeo-builder, journalctl -u rodeo-builder a normal user ~/.config/systemd/user/rodeo-builder.service systemctl --user status rodeo-builder, journalctl --user -u rodeo-builder

A user service runs while that user is logged in; loginctl enable-linger keeps it running without a session.

To turn it off, re-run the installer with --no-builder (or RODEO_BUILDER=0): it stops, disables and removes the unit. systemctl disable --now rodeo-builder works too, but the next install without --no-builder turns it back on. macOS and machines without systemd get no service; run rodeo builder by hand there.

docs.title: Settings page
docs.text:
The builder's Settings page (see Rodeo Builder) is served by rodeo builder itself, on its own address and port. As root on Linux, in both roles, the installer only prepares its login:

Path What /etc/rodeo-builder/htpasswd Login file: users who may add or delete credentials (a link to lab-builder's /etc/lab-builder/htpasswd, created empty when missing)

Add users with rodeo logins add <user> (list, remove). The file is in htpasswd format and the hashes are bcrypt, checked by rodeo itself: no Apache tool is needed, and htpasswd -B lines work too. A user made with htpasswd -m (APR1-MD5) can log in and moves to bcrypt the next time its password is set; any other hash (SHA-1, crypt) cannot log in until the password is set again. Without the system file, on a laptop or a non-root install, rodeo builder uses ~/.rodeo/builder/htpasswd.

Earlier versions served the page through Apache; an update removes what they installed for it (/srv/www/rodeo-builder/, /usr/local/sbin/rodeo-builder-helper, /etc/sudoers.d/rodeo-builder and the rodeo-builder.conf in Apache's conf.d, reloading a running Apache). The login file stays.

docs.title: From a checkout (if you change rodeo itself)
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/avaleror/rodeo-cli.git ~/GitHub/rodeo-cli
cd ~/GitHub/rodeo-cli
bash install.sh --dev        # editable install with the dev extras, in place

The install is editable, so whatever branch is checked out in that directory is what rodeo runs.

docs.title: AWS credentials (both platforms)
docs.text:
rodeo uses boto3 and never reads keys from workshop.yaml or rodeo-plan.yaml. Any standard AWS credential source works: aws login (console session, used by SUSE accounts), aws sso login, ~/.aws/credentials, or environment variables.

aws login
aws sts get-caller-identity             # confirm before provisioning anything

aws login sessions need the awscrt package, which the [aws] extra installs (boto3[crt]). Without it every AWS call fails with MissingDependencyException. These sessions can also throw a transient CreateOAuth2Token error mid-command while still being valid: re-run the command.

docs.title: Differences and things to know
docs.text:
Topic Linux macOS Installer install.sh (KVM host on SLES 16 / Leap 16, control machine elsewhere) install.sh (control machine) Python Distribution python3 3.10+, else a private one via uv Homebrew's if present, else a private one via uv (system python3 is 3.9) [aws] extra Installed on control machines Installed Local labs (no --target aws, gcp, or remote) Yes, on a KVM host No SSH OpenSSH Built-in OpenSSH; nothing extra needed rodeo's own SSH key ~/.rodeo/ssh/id_ed25519, created on first use; AWS labs get their own key in ~/.rodeo/ssh/labs/<lab>/, deleted with the lab Same

Your laptop's public IP. A rodeo-managed AWS security group only admits the public IP of the machine that last ran provision (or up --target aws). Changing network (another Wi-Fi, a VPN, tethering) locks you out: SSH and rodeo fleet time out. Re-run rodeo fleet provision -f workshop.yaml (or rodeo up --target aws again): it reuses the hosts and moves the rule to your new IP. It also closes any student ports, so run rodeo fleet open-access -f workshop.yaml again afterwards.

Laptop sleep during long runs. A deploy runs on the hosts (in tmux), so a sleeping laptop does not break it. What stops are the commands that follow it from your machine, such as rodeo fleet portal publish --watch. Keep the machine awake while they run:

# macOS
caffeinate -i rodeo fleet portal publish --watch -f workshop.yaml
# Linux (systemd)
systemd-inhibit --what=sleep rodeo fleet portal publish --watch -f workshop.yaml

If the watch stops anyway, just start it again: labs that are already published stay published, and the instructor page warns when updates stop arriving.

The same goes for a single-host rodeo up --target aws: if the laptop loses the session (sleep, Wi-Fi, Ctrl-C), the deploy keeps running on the host. Its log is /root/.rodeo/logs/aws-up.log there (rodeo ssh, then sudo tail -f it). Running rodeo up again while that deploy is still going stops with exit 75 instead of starting a second one.

Which rodeo runs where. Your local checkout only drives the control side. KVM hosts install rodeo from GitHub: the same release your laptop runs, main when your laptop runs a checkout between releases, or the ref you pass with --ref / lab.ref. A local change reaches the hosts only after it is pushed. The one exception is the claim portal: rodeo fleet portal up copies the portal code from your local checkout to the portal VM.

Scripts around rodeo. macOS ships BSD tools and zsh, not GNU tools and bash. Commands you write around rodeo may behave differently: there is no timeout (brew install coreutils gives gtimeout), sed -i needs sed -i '', and zsh does not word-split unquoted variables. rodeo itself does not depend on any of these on the control machine.

docs.title: MCP server
docs.text:
rodeo mcp exposes rodeo to MCP clients — Claude Code, editors, agent runtimes — over the MCP stdio transport (newline-delimited JSON-RPC 2.0). It has no extra dependency: the protocol is implemented in rodeo/mcp/.

Every tool runs the rodeo CLI itself, so the surface covers native phase pipelines (suse-virt, rancher, suse-edge, suse-telco) and external engines (lab-in-a-box, plugin-provided types) through the same commands an operator types.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
rodeo mcp --list-tools                      # what would be offered
rodeo mcp                                   # read-only server
rodeo mcp --allow-write --lab-dir ~/rodeo-labs/harvester
Option What it does --allow-write Also offer the lifecycle tools. Off by default, so the server cannot deploy, clean or destroy anything. --lab-dir DIR Default lab directory for lab-scoped tools. Without it, the detected lab dir is used, else the working directory. --list-tools Print the offered tools and exit.

Lab-scoped tools also take a per-call lab_dir argument, which overrides the server default — rodeo commands are lab-directory relative.

docs.title: Limit the server to listed labs
docs.text:
rodeo lab add ~/rodeo-labs/harvester    # needs a terminal
rodeo lab list
rodeo lab remove ~/rodeo-labs/harvester # needs a terminal

rodeo lab add writes the lab's realpath to ~/.rodeo/labs.yaml (mode 0600). Once that file exists, even with an empty list, every path an MCP tool receives must resolve to a listed lab or a path inside one: lab_dir (or the server default), rodeo_up dir, rodeo_init target_dir, rodeo_instances_list dir, rodeo_new from_zip and from_lab_json, and fleet file. Symlinks and .. are resolved first, and a relative path counts from the tool's lab directory. rodeo_new from_base then takes bundled profile names only, no URL. A lab-scoped tool also needs rodeo-plan.yaml or definition.yaml in that directory itself, because rodeo would otherwise fall back to a parent lab or the last lab used (rodeo_init, and rodeo_up with dir, may seed an empty one). A refused call is a tool error and runs nothing.

Without the file the server keeps today's behaviour, accepts any directory and prints one warning on stderr when it starts.

The list is ordinary user data: it stops an MCP client or a confused model from pointing tools at other directories, not a process running as the same user, which can edit the file.

docs.title: Register it with a client
docs.text:
Claude Code (~/.claude.json or project .mcp.json):

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "rodeo": {
      "command": "rodeo",
      "args": ["mcp", "--allow-write", "--lab-dir", "/root/rodeo-labs/harvester"]
    }
  }
}

Drop --allow-write for an agent that should only observe a lab.

docs.title: Keep the agent on the MCP tools: rodeo agent-setup
docs.text:
An agent with a shell can skip the MCP server and type rodeo up or sudo virsh destroy itself. rodeo agent-setup writes a Claude Code kit into the lab that catches this mistake:

cd ~/rodeo-labs/harvester
rodeo agent-setup            # writes .claude/settings.json
rodeo agent-setup --check    # exit 1 if the kit is missing

It merges into <lab>/.claude/settings.json:

  • permissions.deny: Bash(rodeo), Bash(rodeo *), Bash(sudo *), Bash(virsh *), and Bash(ssh *HOST*) / Bash(scp *HOST*) for every VM name, VM address, VIP and AWS host the plan names.
  • A PreToolUse hook on Bash (python -I .../rodeo/agent_guard.py) that also catches the chained forms (cd lab && rodeo up, bash -c '...', $(rodeo status)) and tells the model to use the MCP tools instead.

Your own rules and hooks are kept, odd or invalid JSON is refused rather than overwritten, a symlinked settings file or .claude directory is refused, and a second run changes nothing. Re-run it after the lab's hosts change (a new AWS host, for example): new host rules are added and rodeo's hook entry is updated in place. .claude/ is not part of the lab hash, so writing the kit does not untrust a lab.

This is a mistake filter, not a security boundary. It is a settings file the same user can edit or delete, so it stops a confused model, not a hostile one.

MCP local deploys (rodeo_up, rodeo_deploy and the other write tools that need root) still need NOPASSWD sudo for the user running the MCP server. The kit only denies sudo in the agent's shell, not in the server.

rodeo doctor shows whether the kit is installed in the current lab (and rodeo doctor --output json carries it as agent_kit). It can tell that the kit is installed, not whether an agent session is running without it (when doctor itself runs from a Claude Code shell without the kit, it says so). Only Claude Code has a kit today. When doctor finds a Gemini CLI or Codex CLI config, it reports "no kit for this client".

docs.title: Tools
docs.text:
Read-only (always offered):

Tool rodeo command rodeo_version rodeo --version rodeo_help rodeo [COMMAND] --help — discover commands with no tool of their own rodeo_engines registered lab types, each tagged native or external (JSON) rodeo_doctor rodeo doctor rodeo_profiles rodeo profiles rodeo_plan rodeo plan (output: json for one JSON object, see below) rodeo_status rodeo status; cloud: true runs rodeo status --cloud (the AWS or GCP host, or the KVM host when the plan says deployment_target: remote) rodeo_list rodeo list rodeo_logs rodeo logs --no-follow rodeo_instances_list rodeo instances list rodeo_fleet_status rodeo fleet status rodeo_fleet_doctor rodeo fleet doctor rodeo_preflight rodeo deploy --check — validate, deploy nothing

Lifecycle (only with --allow-write):

Tool rodeo command rodeo_up rodeo up --yes --no-tmux; for target aws it adds --detach (see below). gcp and remote do not, yet. rodeo_deploy rodeo deploy --no-tui (from_phase resumes a phase) rodeo_init rodeo init rodeo_new rodeo new rodeo_start, rodeo_stop, rodeo_start_if_needed, rodeo_restart VM power rodeo_clean rodeo clean --yes — destructive rodeo_destroy rodeo destroy --yes — destructive rodeo_set_password rodeo set-password rodeo_install_extensions rodeo install-extensions rodeo_self_update rodeo self-update

Every tool is non-interactive: no TUI, no tmux wrap, no prompts, no colour. A failing command comes back as a tool error carrying rodeo's exit code and the tail of its output, never as a protocol error.

A call that times out or that the client cancels (notifications/cancelled) stops its whole process group: SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after 5 seconds. Write tools that need root re-exec through sudo, so their rodeo and its ansible-playbook/ssh children run as root, out of the server's reach. sudo relays the SIGTERM to that root rodeo, which stops the processes it started (its descendants, plus its process group when it leads one) with SIGKILL after 3 seconds for anything that ignores SIGTERM, and exits. It never signals the rest of a group it only inherited, such as the script or timeout that ran sudo rodeo. Local deploys from MCP need NOPASSWD sudo, since there is no terminal to type a password in.

docs.title: Plan as JSON
docs.text:
rodeo plan --output json (MCP: rodeo_plan with output: json) prints one object: schema (1), name, type, host_reachable, creates, changes (kind is memory, vcpu or dhcp, with from and to), unchanged, foreign_vms, network, storage (image_dir, downloads), phases (state is done, drift, guarded, pending or failed), phases_pending, summary and config_error. A plan that fails to load prints only {"schema": 1, "error": "..."}.

The object holds no credential values: plan resolves no ?? placeholder, never reads secrets.yaml or the lab secrets file, and masks the plan's own literal credential values and any user:password@ in a URL. The exit code follows the text output: 2 when deploy would refuse the plan (an untrusted lab, an invalid value), even though the JSON was printed. A ?? source in a trusted lab is deferred to deploy and is not a failure.

docs.title: Plugin tools
docs.text: A plugin (a rodeo.plugins entry point) adds tools with rodeo.mcp.tools.register_mcp_tool(tool, mutating=..., lab_scoped=...). Both flags are required. A built-in name, or a name another plugin took, is refused: plugins can't replace a built-in tool. A mutating plugin tool is offered only with --allow-write, and every plugin tool goes through the lab list above (lab_dir when lab-scoped, plus each Arg declared with path="path").

docs.title: rodeo_up on AWS returns a pid
docs.text:
An AWS deploy takes one to two hours. When the target is aws (the target parameter, else the plan's deployment_target), rodeo_up passes --detach: rodeo provisions the EC2 host, starts rodeo up there and returns one JSON object, {"state": "started", "pid", "start", "log", "host"}. The deploy keeps running on the host. Follow it with rodeo_status and cloud: true, which reports running, exited with the exit code, gone (killed or the host rebooted) or none, plus the tail of the log. A deploy that is already running there comes back as a tool error carrying {"state": "already_running", "pid", "log", "host"} (rodeo exit 75).

On the CLI, --detach also works for gcp and for remote (a KVM host you already own, since v0.33.0). rodeo status --cloud reads that run. The log files are aws-up.log, gcp-up.log, or remote-up.log, each with a .pid and a .exit beside it. The MCP tool does not pass --detach for gcp or remote, and its target enum is baremetal, instruqt, or aws. A gcp or remote plan still deploys. The call blocks until the host finishes. rodeo_status with cloud: true does follow the CLI, so a detached gcp or remote run can be read from here once it exists.

A local baremetal deploy has no detach. rodeo_up blocks until it ends, within the server's timeout.

docs.title: Adding a tool
docs.text: Add a row to READ_TOOLS or WRITE_TOOLS in rodeo/mcp/tools.py: the rodeo subcommand, its typed Args, and any fixed flags. Schema, dispatch and the write gate follow from that row — rodeo/mcp/server.py needs no change.

docs.title: Lab player
docs.text:
The rodeo player gives each student one browser window for their lab: the chapter text on the left, then tabs for a terminal, Harvester and Rancher, plus Check, Next and Skip. It runs the SUSE Virtualization Rodeo track (suse-virt-rodeo) on your own cloud labs, with the same setup, check and solve scripts the track already has.

It is opt-in. Nothing in rodeo runs it unless you call rodeo player or rodeo fleet player-setup. Any lab profile can use it: what the player shows comes from the profile's player.yaml (see Player profiles). Today virt-rodeo is the profile that ships one.

docs.title: How it fits together
docs.text:
On each lab host:

  • rodeo-player serves the page and runs the chapter scripts, on loopback only.
  • rodeo-player-ttyd is the browser terminal, as the unprivileged student user.
  • rodeo-player-caddy is the only public listener (port 443). Every request goes through the player's login first, then to the player, the terminal, Harvester or Rancher.

A student signs in once with their lab link (/enter?t=...). The link is a secret: anyone who has it can use that lab. Students can come from any network and any IP: the link is the lock, not the address. After 20 wrong links in 10 minutes from one address, that address gets "Too many tries" (HTTP 429) for a while, so a bot cannot load the lab host by hammering /enter.

docs.title: What the student sees
docs.text:
1. Lobby, on the first visit: each part of the lab (one row per tab) as it comes up, and the chapters ahead. Enter lab turns on when every part answers; after 90 seconds a "Continue anyway" link appears.
  2. Chapter cover, the first time a chapter is opened in that browser: chapter number and name, the one-line mission (teaser), how many tasks, the level (difficulty), Start mission, then the chapter's story.
  3. Working view: the lab takes the screen. A narrow rail on the left has one button per step. The guide opens as a resizable panel next to the lab or folds away; when folded, a small card shows the current step and the chapter's main button.
  4. Guide: the credentials card, one card per step, and "About this chapter" at the end. Code blocks have Copy and Paste in terminal (it types the command at the prompt and never presses Enter). A failed check shows in the step where it was run, with what the check printed.
  5. Chapter complete, after a pass: what was done, what comes next, and the chapter's "why it matters" and links.

The header shows the chapter trail, a "Lab healthy" indicator (the host checks each tab every 30 seconds while the page is open) and the theme switch. Step ticks, covers seen and the guide's width are kept in the student's browser; progress through the chapters is kept on the lab.

docs.title: Writing a track for the player
docs.text:
The player reads the structure authors already write, so any rodeo track works. Split each chapter's assignment.md with top-level headings (a line underlined with ===, or # Title):

Heading Becomes Chapter N: Name, first in the file, plus the text up to the next heading The chapter cover and its story a heading with Credentials in it The credentials card Task N: ... or Step N: ... One step each Bonus ... or a title ending in (optional) An optional step Why ... "Why it matters" on the chapter complete screen More information, Learn more, Resources Links on the chapter complete screen anything else Shown with the step that follows it

Leading emoji in headings are left out of the rail and the cover. A chapter with no task headings is shown as a single step, so older tracks still work. The front matter's teaser and difficulty fill the cover.

docs.title: Every fleet is a workshop
docs.text:
rodeo fleet gives students the player and nothing else: no SSH, no UI ports on the internet. fleet open-access opens 443 only, the UIs sit behind the player's lab login, and the portal hands out one "Open your lab" link per lab.

What decides it, for each fleet:

Fleet Player AWS, lab profile with a player.yaml yes, by default player: false in workshop.yaml, or fleet up --no-player no: students get the UI URLs and passwords kvm-hosts profile no: KVM clusters for operators, not students a profile with no player.yaml (custom, lab-in-a-box) no, unless asked for, and then an error GCP (and any cloud whose provider has supports_player = False) no, for now static hosts (no provider:) only with a player: block

A profile with a track gets its chapters. A profile without one gets the lab tabs, a terminal and the credentials, with the guide folded; the guide panel has a button to the workshop guide when the profile names one (guide_url). Credentials (from the profile's credentials:) are always under Credentials in the header.

The student's terminal runs as student: no sudo, cannot read /root. New fleets get per_host_ssh_key: true, so root on one lab opens no other.

docs.title: One lab, test mode
docs.text:
For a quick test on one lab you do not need a domain. Names are <ip-dashed>.sslip.io and Caddy uses its own CA, so the tester trusts that CA in their browser.

sudo rodeo player setup --track-ref <40-char suse-virt-rodeo commit>   # a profile with a track
sudo rodeo player setup --profile virt-workshop                           # one without
sudo rodeo player link        # prints the lab link
sudo rodeo player test        # solves every chapter: run it last

sslip.io is on the Public Suffix List, so this mode is for testers only, never for students.

docs.title: How long a check may run
docs.text:
Each chapter check is stopped after 120 seconds and counts as a failed check. A track whose checks wait for something slow (a VM booting, a migration) can allow more, from 10 to 3600 seconds:

sudo rodeo player setup --track-ref <sha> --check-timeout 300            # one lab
rodeo fleet player-setup -f workshop.yaml --track-ref <sha> --check-timeout 300   # every lab

The value lands in the player config (/etc/rodeo-player/config.json, check_timeout); rodeo player test uses the same value.

docs.title: A fleet with your own domain
docs.text:
For students, use a DNS zone you own in Route 53 (not on the Public Suffix List) and one wildcard certificate per event. Without one, fleet up warns and runs in test mode: browsers do not trust Caddy's own CA, so the lab tabs stay blank. Add a player: block to workshop.yaml (or pass fleet up --player-domain <zone> when it writes a new one):

player:
  domain: rodeocli.com      # a public Route 53 hosted zone in the fleet's AWS account
  acme_email: you@example.com   # optional, for Let's Encrypt expiry mail
  # staging: true           # first try: Let's Encrypt staging (untrusted, no rate limit)
provider:
  per_host_ssh_key: true    # one root key per lab (fleet up writes it for new workshops)
portal:
  enabled: true             # the portal hands out each lab's link

Each lab gets a random 8-character id and one name per UI under the zone: <id> for the player, then <ui>-<id> for each product UI in the profile's player.yaml (hv-<id> and rancher-<id> for virt-rodeo).

One command does the whole run, and a failed run resumes with the same command:

rodeo fleet up -f workshop.yaml --track-ref <sha> --images-bucket <private image bucket>
rodeo fleet up -f workshop.yaml                  # a profile without a track needs neither

It waits until every lab is ready, then fetches the images, writes the lab names, reuses or issues the certificate, installs the player, opens 443 and publishes the labs. --images-bucket is only for tracks that need private images. The same steps one by one:

rodeo fleet provision   -f workshop.yaml
rodeo fleet deploy      -f workshop.yaml
rodeo fleet lab-images  -f workshop.yaml --bucket <private image bucket> --run
rodeo fleet dns         -f workshop.yaml   # ids + A records
rodeo fleet cert        -f workshop.yaml   # *.<zone>, once per event
rodeo fleet player-setup -f workshop.yaml --track-ref <sha>   # --track-ref only with a track
rodeo fleet open-access -f workshop.yaml   # opens 443 only
rodeo fleet portal publish -f workshop.yaml

The claim portal gets its own name there too, portal-<id>.<zone>, with a random id per portal (written as portal.labels.portal_id, re-picked if the name already exists), so several portals can run at once without sharing or guessing names. fleet portal up writes its record before installing, and Caddy on the portal gets the certificate for that one name. An explicit portal.hostname still wins.

rodeo fleet destroy also removes the lab names (and the portal's, unless --keep-portal) from the zone.

Before a lab is open to students, the operator's own address can already reach its player on 443 (like the UI ports), to check it.

lab-images signs S3 links on your laptop, and a link dies with the credentials that signed it. aws login credentials live about 15 minutes, so fetch the images right after the deploy with --run. Without --run, the command refuses when your credentials end within the hour.

docs.title: DNS records
docs.text:
Route 53 cannot tag a single record, so every name rodeo writes also gets a TXT record of the same name:

"managed-by=rodeo fleet=<workshop name> host=<host id> region=<aws region>"

That TXT is how rodeo knows a name is its own:

  • fleet dns refuses a name that already holds anything rodeo did not mark for that lab, and changes nothing for that lab.
  • fleet dns --delete and fleet destroy delete only names marked for this workshop. Records you made by hand are never touched.
  • Re-runs are safe. A lab with a new address gets its records moved.
  • A lab the dead-man switch terminated never runs fleet destroy, so its names would stay behind, pointing at an AWS address someone else may get next. fleet dns, fleet up and fleet destroy first prune every rodeo-marked name (any workshop) whose address is not a live rodeo instance in the mark's region. fleet dns --prune does only that. If the instance list cannot be read, nothing is pruned.

Your AWS identity needs route53:ListHostedZonesByName, ListResourceRecordSets, ChangeResourceRecordSets and GetChange on the zone, plus ec2:DescribeInstances for the prune.

docs.title: The certificate
docs.text:
rodeo fleet cert runs on your laptop. It downloads a pinned lego release once (checked against a sha256 in rodeo), then gets *.<zone> from Let's Encrypt with a DNS-01 challenge in your zone. lego gets your current AWS credentials as short-lived environment variables, so an aws login session works. The files stay in ~/.rodeo/certs/<zone>/; a re-run reuses the certificate until it is due for renewal.

Let's Encrypt allows 50 certificates per registered domain per week. One wildcard per event keeps you far from that limit. Use staging: true for your first tries.

fleet player-setup pushes the certificate and key to each lab over the SSH session's stdin. On the lab they live in /etc/rodeo-player/tls/, root-only (directory 0700, files 0600). Caddy reads them through systemd LoadCredential, so neither the Caddy user nor the student can open the key file. Lab hosts never run ACME and never get AWS credentials.

docs.title: Player profiles
docs.text:
The player is the same for every SUSE product. What changes per lab sits in a player.yaml next to the lab profile's rodeo-plan.yaml (rodeo/data/examples/<profile>/player.yaml). This is the virt-rodeo one:

title: SUSE Virtualization Rodeo
track_repo: https://github.com/SUSE-Technical-Marketing/suse-virt-rodeo.git  # optional
# guide_url: https://.../workshop-guide/  # without a track: the web guide
kubeconfig: harvester-kubeconfig          # in ~/.rodeo, written by rodeo up (optional)
student_ssh_key: /opt/suse-virt-workshop/lab-vm-key   # optional
uis:
  - key: hv                               # name: hv-<id>.<zone>
    label: SUSE Virtualization (Harvester)
    upstream: 192.168.122.10:443          # on the lab network
    # scheme: http                        # default https (self-signed is fine)
    tab_port: 8443                        # the port the track's tabs use
    # lobby: false                        # the lobby does not wait for this UI
  - key: rancher
    label: SUSE Rancher Prime
    upstream: 192.168.122.9:30002
    tab_port: 30002
credentials:                              # shown under Credentials in the player
  - label: SUSE Rancher Prime
    user: admin
    password: ??rancher_admin_password
variables:                                # track variable: ??secrets.yaml key
  RANCHER_PASSWORD: ??rancher_admin_password
  HARVESTER_PASSWORD: ??harvester_admin_password

Shipped profiles: virt-rodeo, suse-edge and suse-telco (track; edge and telco also keep their web guide as a button), virt-workshop, virt-workshop-2n (web guide), harvester, harvester-2n, rancher-test, rancher-lab-config (no instructions).

  • uis: one to eight product UIs. Each gets its own name, its own Caddy site behind the lab login, and the track tabs on tab_port open it. A track tab with a path (a Gitea repo page, say) opens that page of the UI.
  • lobby: false on a UI the student brings up later in the lab (telco's site consoles after lab 06). The lobby does not probe it, so "Enter lab" does not wait for it.
  • kubeconfig and student_ssh_key: leave them out when the track does not use them. The student gets a copy of each.
  • student_libvirt and student_vm_access: for labs whose guide drives VMs from the host. The first puts the student in the libvirt group with qemu:///system as the default (root-equivalent on that host, so fleet player-setup refuses it without per_host_ssh_key: true). The second makes the student their own key and installs it for root on the listed lab VMs, using root's key, which the student never sees. A fleet that runs the player makes that key before rodeo up, and suse-edge's content phase adds it to the edge3/edge4 EIB definitions, so the nodes the student builds later trust it too. Deploys without the player (self-serve labs, builder images) have no such key and their definitions keep only the host key.
  • student_rodeo_commands: rodeo subcommands the guide runs on the host as root (suse-edge: pull-edge-image, eject-iso). The student's rodeo is a shim that sends exactly those subcommands through sudo -n to a root wrapper (/usr/local/libexec/rodeo-player/rodeo-root), which points SUDO_USER at the user who deployed the lab, so rodeo uses that ~/.rodeo (trust, secrets), never the student's. The guide's commands stay the same. Needs student_libvirt: true, which is already root-equivalent.
  • credentials: what the student signs in with, resolved on the lab into a root-only file the player serves behind the lab login. ??<key> only.
  • variables: passwords the track shows. Always ??<key>, never the password itself.

Both resolve ??<key> the way rodeo up did: the host's ~/.rodeo/secrets.yaml (the deploying user's over root's) and, over it, the lab's own .rodeo-secrets.yaml (suse-telco keeps mgmt_root_password there).

rodeo fleet dns and rodeo fleet player-setup read the profile from lab.profile in workshop.yaml. On one host, pass it yourself:

sudo rodeo player setup --profile <profile> [--track-ref <sha>]

A profile without a player.yaml is an error: the player never borrows another product's UIs. To point a UI at another address on a single lab, use --upstream <ui>=<ip>:<port>.

docs.title: Releasing and validation
docs.text:
Users install rodeo with one command, and that command has to give them a version that works. A tagged release isn't proof of that: some breakages only show up on a real deploy. So rodeo has two steps: release (automatic) and validation (a live deploy, then a reviewed PR).

Who installs it STABLE (a file on main, one tag such as v0.32.2) install.sh by default, rodeo self-update by default, and GitHub's "Latest" badge A newer tag that isn't in STABLE yet only --ref vX.Y.Z main only --ref main / self-update --branch main

A KVM or cloud host that rodeo sets up installs the same release as the laptop driving it, so validating a release covers both sides.

docs.title: 1. Release
docs.text:
release-please keeps a release PR open on main. Merging it creates the tag and the GitHub release. The new release is not the default yet. The release workflow puts the "Latest" badge back on the STABLE release, so the releases page shows what users actually get.

Before merging the release PR, clean the notes: merge commits list every change twice.

docs.title: 2. Validate
docs.text:
From a laptop with AWS credentials (aws login):

scripts/smoke-aws.sh v0.33.0                # rancher-test: about 15 min, under 1 USD

It deploys rancher-test on a fresh EC2 host running exactly that tag, follows it with rodeo status --cloud, destroys the host whatever happens, and writes smoke-v0.33.0-rancher-test.md. Exit 0 means the deploy finished with exit 0 and printed "Your lab is up".

Then test what the release changed. If it touched a profile or a workshop, deploy that one too and walk its checks, for example scripts/smoke-aws.sh v0.33.0 virt-workshop. Every evidence file goes in the promotion PR.

docs.title: 3. Promote
docs.text:
scripts/promote-stable.sh v0.33.0 smoke-v0.33.0-rancher-test.md [more.md ...]

It refuses evidence without a PASS, writes the tag to STABLE on a new branch, and opens chore(stable): promote v0.33.0 with the evidence as the body. A second person reviews and merges it. From that merge on, new installs and self-update get the release, and GitHub's "Latest" badge moves to it.

docs.title: Rolling back
docs.text: If a promoted release turns out broken, revert the promotion PR. STABLE goes back to the previous release, new installs get that one, and rodeo self-update takes anyone already on the broken release back to it.

docs.title: Why a file
docs.text: STABLE is read from the clone install.sh already makes: no GitHub API call, so no rate limit for a room full of students behind one IP. Promoting is a reviewed PR, so the history says who promoted what and with which evidence. release-please is untouched.

docs.title: Rodeo Builder
docs.text:
→ Open the Rodeo Builder

The Rodeo Builder composes a new rodeo in the browser: pick the lab engine, put story chapters in order, tag their text for translation and with story ids, and download the result as a profile you install with rodeo.

It comes in two versions of the same page:

  • Published (the button above): a static page built by GitHub Actions with the docs. Nothing you do there leaves your browser; you download a zip.
  • Live, installed with rodeo-cli: rodeo builder serves the page on your machine, reads its data live and adds Save to profiles, which writes the rodeo straight into ~/.rodeo/profiles/<name>/.
rodeo builder                 # opens http://127.0.0.1:8678/
rodeo up --profile <name>     # after Save to profiles

On Linux with systemd the installer already runs it as rodeo-builder.service, listening on every interface, so the page is up on https://<host>:8678/ without starting it; see Install (--no-builder turns it off, --builder-host 127.0.0.1 keeps it local). With --host 0.0.0.0 (or ::) rodeo builder answers to the machine's own host names and interface addresses, read at each start, plus any --allow-host.

docs.title: What you compose
docs.text:
• Lab engine. The engines are the rodeo types installed (a plugin's included); the deployment targets and instructions formats offered are the ones rodeo knows, never a fixed list. suse-virt, rancher and suse-edge are rodeo's own engines, under the native card; lab-in-a-box (and any other external engine) is a card beside it. Picking native shows an Engine row (suse-virt, rancher, suse-edge); picking an engine shows a Profile row, every bundled profile of that engine's type with its size, the default first; the rodeo's plan starts from the profile picked. The (i) on an engine shows its size, its profiles and what it provides (for example Harvester, KubeVirt, Longhorn, Rancher, Fleet). For suse-virt the profiles are harvester (the default), harvester-2n, harvester-ha, test and the workshop profiles. lab-in-a-box builds any lab lab-in-a-box can; picking it shows a Lab row:
    • create (the default) opens the lab-builder inside the page, empty; "Send this lab" there hands the lab back.
    • modify opens the lab-builder inside the page with this rodeo's lab loaded. It is greyed out, "no lab selected", until the rodeo has a lab.
    • examples shows an Example row: one list of the bundled lab-in-a-box rodeos (smlm-workshop) and the example labs the lab-in-a-box checkout offers, both the ones the release ships and the host's own (EXAMPLE_LABS_DIR, by default /etc/lab_creation/examples). Only what the release ships carries a star and its version; a release too old to say where an example comes from carries none. Each card carries the name and the node and cluster count only; a filter box narrows the list and it folds after eight. The box below the rows shows the chosen lab's description and add-ons. An example lab is taken like an uploaded lab file, so it lands in the plan as lab_in_a_box.lab; a bundled rodeo stays selected on every tab, so its lab is the one the lab-builder opens. Every mode's box offers Open embedded lab-builder, which opens the lab-builder inside this page on the lab that mode is about (nothing for create, the rodeo's lab for modify, the example picked for examples), and Upload lab, a lab definition file as lab-in-a-box reads them (JSON or YAML; the page parses YAML with the bundled vendor/js-yaml.min.js, MIT). create and modify also offer Open lab-builder ↗, the lab-builder in its own tab with this rodeo's lab filled in (only its add-ons when the lab is too large for a link); download the lab there and upload it here to bring it back.

Provides lists what the lab offers chapters, from lab-in-a-box's whole catalogue: add-ons, Kubernetes clusters (rke2, k3s, ...) and infrastructure (such as pxe). Type a name to add one. Add-ons go into the generated plan; Kubernetes clusters and infrastructure are set up in the lab-builder (Embed here), whose lab brings them back. With a lab, it lists that lab's add-ons (on VMs and Kubernetes clusters), Kubernetes cluster types and infrastructure.

A lab brought back (sent, or uploaded as a JSON or YAML lab file) becomes the plan's lab_in_a_box.lab (see the plan reference); the rest of the plan, such as an imported workshop's variants and workshop: block, is kept. Its add-ons are then edited in the lab-builder.

No credential from that lab reaches the plan. Values of password, token, registration code, API key and secret key fields become ??<field> placeholders, and those placeholders are added to the plan's operator_secrets, so rodeo up asks for them once; the toast names them. Node names and addresses written literally in add-on settings (for example client_registration_server: smlm.rodeo.lab) become ${node_fqdn:smlm} / ${node_ip:smlm}, which rodeo fills with each host's and instance's values; settings unchanged from the lab the rodeo already had stay as written. Addresses that look like the lab's but belong to no node are listed in the panel to check.

With a lab, the panel lists its nodes (address, vCPU, RAM, add-ons, cluster) and Kubernetes clusters, read-only, and flags what rodeo deploys but does not fully drive: Harvester nodes and PXE-booted nodes. It also lists the lab's fields the builder's lab-in-a-box release doesn't know (its schema is read with the catalogue), which rodeo up would refuse. On the command line, rodeo new <name> --from-lab-json <file> does the same import. - Start from a workshop. Above the chapter library, a list of whole workshops to start a rodeo from: the bundled examples, the chapter sources that come with a profile, every published rodeo in the catalog, and the bundled lab-in-a-box rodeos (also under the lab engine's examples row). Start from replaces the rodeo's lab and chapters with the workshop's: its lab engine and profile (for example suse-virt with the virt-workshop profile, whose extra setup the exercises need) and all its chapters (Undo restores them). A catalog rodeo is fetched when you start from it, so it brings everything it was published with: its plan, its lab-in-a-box lab, its chapters with their checks, and its translations, language branches included. The published page can't fetch it; there its entry shows rodeo new <name> --from <repo>. - Chapters. The library lists every workshop's chapters, to add to the rodeo: the bundled examples' story/ directories, the workshops whose chapters live in their own repository (listed in rodeo/builder/chapter_sources.yaml: the SMLM workshop's Instruqt track, the SUSE Virtualization Rodeo's Instruqt track and the Virtualization workshop's exercises; each entry's ref is a branch, a tag or a full commit id, to pin a release; an entry without engine and profile, for a repository with chapters but no rodeo-cli settings, only adds its chapters to the library, and no rodeo starts from it), the story/ of every published rodeo in the catalog (rodeo/data/catalog.d/, unless chapter_sources.yaml already names its repository; its translations come along, from story/strings/ and from each language branch, so adding one of its chapters adds the translations of its spans you don't have yet), and the chapters you create with + New. Workshops start collapsed: click a workshop's title to show its chapters. The (i) next to it (hover, or click to keep it open) shows where the chapters come from, the lab engine and profile they run on, their count and time, and what they need. + all adds its chapters to the rodeo's. A chapter card shows its title; hover over it for its time and needs, or turn on the list button next to the search to show them on every card. The funnel button next to it shows only the workshops for this lab engine, the chapters this lab can run, or the chapters not in the rodeo yet. Drag chapters into the rodeo (anywhere on the list) or click them; click a chapter again to take it out. Click a row in the rodeo to insert new chapters after it instead of at the end. Reorder by dragging or with Alt+↑/↓. Removing a chapter or a span offers Undo for a few seconds. When every chapter comes from workshops that run on one other engine, a banner offers to switch to it. A chapter that needs something the lab doesn't provide is marked, and for lab-in-a-box one click adds the missing add-on. Chapters that come with a check script bring it along. A new chapter's Requires from the lab field suggests, as you type, what an engine really provides: the native engines' capabilities and lab-in-a-box's catalogue (add-ons, infrastructure services, Kubernetes cluster types). If the lab-in-a-box catalogue could not be read, the page says why. The rodeo builder server reads the catalogue and the lab schema once per checkout and again only when the checkout's files change. While the page starts, a note says it is loading; if the page can't start (a script error, the builder data not loading) the note says why and offers Reload, and after 30 s it names the calls still waiting for the server. When nothing matches, Enter adds what you typed as a new need: a placeholder for something no engine provides yet, like missing_addon. Such a need only marks the chapter as "work needed" (also listed, by name, in the download's README); it never blocks the rodeo and never reaches the lab. - Import. Import above the library adds a workshop from a URL: a git repository or a directory in one (https://<host>/<owner>/<repo>/tree/<ref>/<dir>). The builder detects the format (a rodeo story/, an Instruqt track <dir>/*/assignment.md, or markdown <dir>/*.md) and lists its chapters as a new group; × removes the group again. The published page reads public github.com repositories through the GitHub API (60 unauthenticated requests an hour); the rodeo builder server clones any public https repository (shallow and sparse, no credentials). Imported groups are kept with the draft. - Story. Edit on a chapter opens the story editor (rows with span warnings show how many). Select text and click Tag selection, use the toolbar, or press Alt+T / Alt+I / Alt+N to mark it Translatable, Don't translate or No-lang. Story (Alt+S) marks the text students get retold: it takes the chapter's story, or asks for the story's name, offering the one the other chapters tell. When the chapters tell more than one story, Review warns and offers Make all the same story. Double-click a span to change its type, language, id or story id. Ids follow rmstory's rules (<chapter>.N, <parent>.N when nested) and the editor shows the same warnings as rmstory validate. The source and the preview sit side by side and scroll together; the preview renders the chapter as Markdown or HTML (only safe tags, images as links), with its spans marked. Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Shift+Z undo and redo; Cancel closes the editor and discards its changes, Done keeps them. - Translations. The story editor's translations tab lists every translatable span per language of the rodeo. Add new language… (there, or at the end of the rodeo tab's Language list, which shows only the rodeo's own languages) asks for its code (es, pt-br: named like the language branch Publish puts it in) and starts it empty, as a draft copy of another translation or, on the live page, translated with an rmstory engine; it can also become the rodeo's language (story.language). Click a cell to write or review a translation; a nested span stays in it as <span id="..."/>. The download carries them in rmstory's translation store, story/strings/, and rodeo story render --language <lang> uses them (with --engine for the spans still missing).

Review and download (step 03) checks the rodeo before you download it: the lab covers every chapter, the span ids are valid (each warning has a Fix button), the exact files in the zip (listed when you click N files in .zip), and the commands to install it, ready to copy. Missing lab features and span warnings never block the download.

Every warning and error the page shows has a × that closes it, and Esc closes the message at the bottom of the page. Closing one means "read", not "fixed": the counts above it still report it, a warning that says something else still shows, and a reload shows them all again.

The page keeps a draft of your rodeo in this browser. After a reload it offers to restore it.

docs.title: With rmstory on the live builder
docs.text:
When rmstory is installed where rodeo builder runs (sudo rodeo install-deps --story), the live page also uses it:

  • Translate missing (translations tab): fills the chosen language's missing translations with an rmstory engine (rmstory extract --engine <e> --to <lang>). They are stored as draft; what you wrote or reviewed is kept. rmstory also gives unnamed spans an id (<chapter>.N).
  • Validate (step 03): rmstory's own validate on the chapters.
  • Draft with an engine (New chapter): an engine that can generate text (rmstory engines says "translate + generate", for example claude-code, ollama or gemini) drafts the chapter from your description, told what the lab provides and which chapters come before it. Its spans are renumbered new-chapter.N; review the draft before you create the chapter.
  • New story (rodeo tab): the same exercises told as a different story. You say what is what with the span tags (story editor):
  • story: spans tagged with a story id (hist): retold;
  • exercise: translatable spans without a story id: translated, never retold;
  • fixed: don't-translate (no) or no-lang spans, and text outside spans: kept word for word.

Say what the new story is about and pick an engine that can generate text; rmstory generate rewrite --theme rewrites the story spans and the exercise spans never reach the engine. The retold chapters (ids <chapter>-<theme>, story span ids <theme>.<id>; exercise and fixed spans keep their ids and translations) become a library group and replace the rodeo's chapters; Undo puts the originals back. They live only in this browser (the page's draft) until you download, save to profiles or publish.

Engines read their keys from the environment rodeo builder runs in (for example DEEPL_AUTH_KEY, GEMINI_API_KEY, RMSTORY_OLLAMA_URL, or a logged-in claude command for claude-code) or from a stored credential: the Settings page stores one per provider (Google Gemini API key, DeepL API key, …), encrypted under its own password. An engine that needs a key and has neither is listed in red as no credential; running it explains how to add one and links to the Settings form with that type chosen. With stored credentials, the page asks which one (when there are several) and its password; the key is decrypted on the server and given only to rmstory, never to the page. Stored credentials work where the deploy dialog's do (a builder on loopback, or behind the web server's login). The published page writes translations by hand only.

The right-hand panel sets the name, story title, language, deployment target and Story told to students (shown when the chapters have spans tagged with a story id: All stories together renders the chapters whole; a story renders only that story's spans, in order), and previews every file of the download. plan.yaml is an editor: change anything and the download keeps it; name, deployment_target and story stay in sync with the rodeo tab, and Reset to generated drops your edits. Changing the lab engine regenerates the plan, after asking.

docs.title: Infrastructure and instructions
docs.text:
The page keeps the lab (Infrastructure: engine, base profile, plan, definition, lab-in-a-box lab) apart from what students read (Instructions: chapters, stories, translations, checks). Step 03 downloads either the whole rodeo (Download: All) or one part: Infrastructure definition only (<name>-infrastructure.zip, installable with rodeo new --from-zip) or Instructions only (<name>-instructions.zip: story/ and checks/, laid out to be pushed as a content repository).

Where students' instructions come from (rodeo tab) is This rodeo's chapters (the default: the chapters in the middle column, story/ in the download) or A repository, which points the plan at instructions kept in their own repository (for example the -instructions one Publish creates); the chapters column then says the deployed instructions come from there. The URL (https://<host>/<owner>/<repo>[/tree/<ref>/<path>]) and format become the plan's content: block. rodeo up renders them after the lab is up, installs the repository's checks/ for every user of the host and runs its custom/scripts/, and rodeo content apply updates them on a running lab without redeploying (see the plan reference).

docs.title: Install what you downloaded
docs.text:
The zip holds one profile directory, <name>/, with rodeo-plan.yaml, the chapters (story/NN-<id>.md), story/chapters.yaml (minutes, needs and check script per chapter), one story/stories/<story id>.yaml per story, checks/check-<id>.sh stubs, a README with the exact commands and, when the rodeo starts from a profile (suse-virt, rancher, suse-edge or an imported lab-in-a-box rodeo), builder.yaml naming that base profile.

rodeo new <name> --from-zip <name>.zip
rodeo up --profile <name>

--from-zip copies the base profile, lays the zip's files over it and writes ~/.rodeo/profiles/<name>/. A new lab-in-a-box rodeo carries its own definition.yaml and needs no base. --from <profile> overrides the base and --force replaces an existing profile. The zip may only hold the files the builder writes; anything else (other paths, links, oversize files) is refused before anything is written. Save to profiles in rodeo builder does the same without the zip.

A published rodeo (see Publish to GitHub) installs the same way from its repository, and a catalog rodeo by its name alone:

rodeo new <name> --from https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>[@<ref>]
rodeo up --profile <catalog name>     # fetched and installed on first use
rodeo profiles                        # lists the catalog too

The repository is fetched shallow, without credentials, and only the files a builder rodeo may hold are installed; ~/.rodeo/profiles/<name>/rodeo.lock records the repository, ref and commit. --force re-fetches.

docs.title: The live builder
docs.text:
rodeo builder serves rodeo/builder/htdocs/ and answers the page's requests with rodeo/builder/api.py (rodeo/builder/server.py, standard library only). It links to and embeds lab-in-a-box's published static lab-builder, or the one --lab-builder-url names. With --start-lab-builder it starts the checkout's own dynamic lab-builder (webui/run-local.py) next to it on --lab-builder-port, opened on the host name the browser used for the builder (the published one when the checkout has none or it can't start). That lab-builder has no login or token, so any site you browse can save labs through it: it is off by default and only allowed on a loopback --host. At start it fetches the chapter sources (a source that can't be fetched is left out, with a warning) and the lab-in-a-box catalogue: --labinabox <checkout>, else RODEO_LABINABOX_PATH, else lab-in-a-box's latest release, fetched into ~/.rodeo/vendor/lab-in-a-box/ the way a deploy does.

On loopback it speaks plain HTTP: nothing leaves the machine. On any other address it speaks HTTPS, with --tls-cert and --tls-key or, without them, a certificate signed by a CA of your own that it makes once in ~/.rodeo/builder/tls/ (ca.pem, key 0600). The certificate names this host's FQDN and short name, its addresses and every --allow-host, and is made again when a name is missing or it has less than 30 days left. Import ca.pem once in each browser, from https://<host>:<port>/ca.pem or the file, and every builder this CA signs for is trusted; until then the browser warns about the certificate. The CA is name-constrained to the domain of the names it was made for, so a later name outside them is reported at start and refused by browsers: remove ca.pem and ca.key to make a new CA (and import it again).

Option Default --host, --port 127.0.0.1, 8678 Where to listen (--port 0 picks a free port). --expose off Required for a non-loopback --host, served over HTTPS: anyone who reaches it can save profiles as you. Publish then uses the github.com pages, never this host's GitHub login; Deploy and stored credentials need a login. --allow-host NAME Extra Host name to accept (the name or IP clients use with --expose); also put in the generated certificate. --tls-cert FILE, --tls-key FILE rodeo's own CA PEM certificate (with its chain) and key to serve HTTPS with: one from your CA, or certbot's fullchain.pem and privkey.pem. --labinabox latest release lab-in-a-box checkout for the catalogue and the lab-builder. --lab-builder-url URL (RODEO_LAB_BUILDER_URL) the published lab-builder A lab-builder you already run (for example on an automation node) for the page to link to and embed; nothing is started. --start-lab-builder off Start the checkout's own dynamic lab-builder. Loopback --host only. --lab-builder-port 8677 Port of the lab-builder --start-lab-builder starts, on the same address as --host. --source ID=CHECKOUT, --no-fetch-sources fetch all Local chapter sources, or none. --open/--no-open open Open the page in a browser.

Writes are guarded: the server only answers requests whose Host is an allowed name (loopback names by default), so other sites can't reach it through DNS rebinding, and Save sends a per-run token that only the served page has. The page runs under a Content-Security-Policy that allows only its own files (the fonts ship in htdocs/fonts/) and the lab-builder frame.

docs.title: Where a rodeo deploys
docs.text:
The Deployment target choice is the plan's deployment_target. The page names the built-ins for what they are: This host (localhost) is baremetal, the host the builder itself runs on — the plan value is unchanged, only the label says where it lands.

A KVM host of mine (SSH) is deployment_target: remote: the builder ships the rodeo to a host you own and runs rodeo up there (see remote_host). It is offered only once you have stored a KVM host (SSH) credential — host, login and private key — on the Settings page, since there is nowhere to deploy without one. The deploy dialog then asks which host, and for that credential's password; the key is written into the lab directory as .rodeo-remote-key (mode 600) and never leaves the builder's host.

docs.title: Deploy without saving
docs.text:
Deploy (header) runs the rodeo on the builder's host exactly as it is on the page, without saving it to your profiles first. It needs root for rodeo up: the builder runs as root or the user has passwordless sudo (sudo -n true). Otherwise, and on the published page, the button is greyed out and says why on hover.

  • On an --expose builder, deploying and using stored credentials need a login from /etc/rodeo-builder/htpasswd: the first Deploy makes the browser ask for it (Cancel leaves the page as it was), and the browser sends it with every request after. The builder checks a login again after 5 minutes. The builder serves plain HTTP, so the login crosses the network unencrypted. On loopback no login is asked.

  • The dialog says plainly that the rodeo is not saved, and offers Save to profiles and deploy next to Deploy without saving.

  • The deploy runs rodeo up --yes --no-tmux --dir <lab> from a copy in ~/rodeo-labs/<name>-unsaved-<UTC time>/ (base profile plus the page's files, as Save lays them out), its output in <lab>/.builder-deploy.log. Secrets rodeo can generate go to the lab's .rodeo-secrets.yaml; ones only you have (operator_secrets) are asked for in the dialog and written to ~/.rodeo/secrets.yaml, never shown again.
  • Log in the banner keeps the deploy's whole output as it runs, up to 100000 lines, and follows the tail unless you scroll up. The page asks only for the bytes it has not seen yet, so a long deploy does not resend its log every poll; the full output is always in <lab>/.builder-deploy.log.
  • A banner stays while it runs and after it ends, with the lab directory, the log, Stop (interrupts rodeo up like Ctrl-C) and Save to profiles, and keeps saying the rodeo is not saved until you save it. Once the deploy is over, × closes the banner; while it runs it has none, because Stop and Log are the only controls a running deploy has. One deploy runs at a time; rerun or resume from the lab directory with rodeo up.

docs.title: Settings and stored credentials
docs.text:
Settings, at the right of the header on the live builder, opens the Settings page in a new tab: /rodeo-builder/settings/ on the builder's own address and port. It keeps the credentials you deploy with — SCC registration codes, registry and Application Collection logins, AWS keys, SSH keys, GitHub tokens, or any key: value fields — encrypted on that host, one file per credential in root's ~/.rodeo/vault/, the store the builder reads.

The page is served by rodeo builder itself and uses its API (GET vault, POST vault-add and vault-delete, with the page's token). Adding or deleting a credential needs a login: the browser asks for a user from the login file (rodeo logins add <user>; bcrypt hashes in htpasswd format, /etc/rodeo-builder/htpasswd or else ~/.rodeo/builder/htpasswd, see Install) the first time, and an --expose builder asks before listing anything. Off loopback the builder speaks HTTPS, so the login and the values never cross the network in the clear.

  • Each credential has its own password, at least 8 characters, asked when it is added, every time it is used and to delete it: a delete with the wrong password is refused. Neither the password nor the values are kept by the page: a table shows each credential's name, application, engine (rodeo for the ones stored here), whether it is encrypted, when it was added and last used, never its values. The application of a rodeo credential is its type.
  • Credentials of other engines are listed and used too, with their engine's name: today the lab-in-a-box engine's, from /etc/lab_creation/credentials/; their application is the part of the file name <application>-<account>.yaml before the first - (aws-tmm.yaml: aws). They are read-only in rodeo (no Delete). One stored without encryption opens without a password; an encrypted one asks for its passphrase.
  • Failed passwords and logins wait longer from the fifth in a row on: 1 minute, then 2, 4, … up to 1 hour between tries. A success resets the count.
  • The same API serves scripts: POST /api?action=vault-add ({name, type, fields, password}) and vault-delete ({id, password}), with the page's X-Rodeo-Builder-Token and an Authorization: Basic login checked against /etc/rodeo-builder/htpasswd. Without a login they answer 401.
  • In the deploy dialog, each secret the lab asks for offers Use stored… with the credentials that can fill it. After the password, the page fills that secret and every other one the same credential provides (an AWS credential fills both aws_access_key_id and aws_secret_access_key). A generic credential fills secrets whose names match its field names.
  • The filled values go where typed ones go: into ~/.rodeo/secrets.yaml for rodeo up. Deleting a stored credential does not remove them from there.
  • The page also lists the keys already in root's ~/.rodeo/secrets.yaml, names only and read-only: rodeo up reads that file directly. In the deploy dialog, Use stored… offers them under secrets.yaml (names sharing a word with the secret first). Picking one asks no password and locks the input ("from secrets.yaml: ", Clear to type instead); the builder copies the value on its host, so it never reaches the browser.

docs.title: Publish to GitHub
docs.text:
